->Or<-

## On the Use of the Spirit of Wine of Lully
<note>original: "Spiritus Vini Lulliani". This refers to a highly concentrated alcohol or "quintessence" named after the medieval philosopher Ramon Lull, which alchemists believed could extract the essence of all things.</note>

->*FOUR BOOKS.*<-

### A Practical Work

Through the harmonies of Philosophers who otherwise
disagree with one another, mutually reconciled
from both the ancient and modern Fathers of
adept <note>An "adept" is someone who has mastered the "Great Work" of alchemy—the transmutation of base metals and the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> Philosophy, collected with the greatest zeal,
and so arranged in a most elegant and new method
that even novices <note>original: "tyrones"</note> can distinguish
counterfeit or fraudulent <note>original: "sophisticas". In this context, it refers to adulterated or fake alchemical recipes designed to trick the unwary.</note> preparations of
vegetables, animals, and minerals from the true ones,
whether for medical or metallic <note>Referring to "chrysopoeia," the art of making gold.</note> purposes,
and thus guard themselves against wandering
deceivers, imaginary processes, and the
squandering of their money.

## ISAAC OF HOLLAND,
<note>Isaacus Hollandus was a name attributed to one or two legendary 15th-century Dutch alchemists whose works were highly influential in the development of chemistry.</note>

<note>original: "Oper. miner." refers to "Opera mineralia." "Th. Chym." refers to the "Theatrum Chemicum," a massive and famous 17th-century compendium of alchemical writings.</note>

> speak to you of selbach, kalcabria, manessi, and of a certain

> the way for you and removed every obstacle, so that 
> you may not wander in error.
<note>Words like "selbach" and "muerach" are "Decknamen" (cover-names)—cryptic, often Arabic-derived jargon used by medieval alchemists to hide their ingredients from the uninitiated. Hollandus claims to be avoiding this "gobbledygook" to speak clearly to the reader.</note>

#### OF THE
## ROYAL SOCIETY
<note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691) was a founding member of the Royal Society and is often called the "Father of Modern Chemistry." Despite his modern reputation, he remained deeply interested in alchemical pursuits throughout his life.</note>

->*Wishing you long life and good health.*<-

The secrets of Paracelsus <note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a Swiss physician and alchemist who argued that the goal of alchemy should be the creation of medicines rather than gold.</note>, though praised by many with so many and such great tributes (which were nonetheless still insufficient), were the reason that ten years ago I began to consult Paracelsus himself regarding his medicines. # ISAAC HOLLAND,

> I have spoken to you in open words, using no parables. If I were to speak to you of *selbach*, *Kalcabria*, *manessi*, and of a certain red thing, or of blue *muerach*, *illabar*, and *calfaria* <note>These terms—selbach, manessi, etc.—are "Decknamen" or cover-names. Alchemists used this gibberish to hide the identity of their chemicals from the "unworthy," a practice the author here is rejecting in favor of plain speech.</note>, or the like, you would not easily understand; but I have opened the way for you and removed every obstacle, so that you may not go astray.

# RIPLEY,

->*Chapter 2 of the Marrow of Chemical Philosophy*<-

> How those menstruums <term>Menstruums: In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a powerful solvent. The term comes from the Latin for "monthly," relating to the cyclical nature of the work. It is the liquid used to dissolve or "open" a solid metal to begin its transformation.</term> may be obtained, which are oily, moist, sulfurous, and mercurial, well-suited to the nature of metals; with which our bodies <note>In alchemical texts, "bodies" almost always refers to the metals themselves (like gold, lead, or antimony) before they have been dissolved or spiritualized.</note> are to be artificially dissolved.

->here<-

We shall demonstrate a clear practice.

The secrets <term>Arcana: From the Latin "arcanum" (secret). In 17th-century chemistry, these were hidden medicinal preparations or "mysteries" believed to hold profound healing powers beyond standard herbal remedies.</term> of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), known as Paracelsus, was a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals and chemicals in medicine, often writing in a notoriously difficult and cryptic style.</note>, though praised by so many with such great honors—which nonetheless feel insufficient—were the reason why, ten years ago, I began to consult Paracelsus himself regarding his medicines. Two years passed from that time, during which I turned his pages <note>original: "versarem manu," literally "turning with the hand," a common expression for diligent, repeated study.</note> day and night, with a spirit nearly tireless and undefeated, yet with uneven success and almost no practical benefit. For in the Paracelsian books, besides that common concealment of secrets customary among the Adepts <term>Adepts: A title for "master" alchemists who had successfully discovered the secrets of the transmutation of matter or the creation of universal medicines.</term>, I found another layer [of obscurity] added, which is less common among—

[the usual difficulty of] the Adepts, but a far greater difficulty, since in those works Paracelsus, the corrector of the Adepts <note>original: "Adeptorum corrector." Paracelsus often positioned himself as a reformer who corrected the errors of previous alchemical and medical authorities.</note>, had set out to instruct regarding his Secrets <term>Arcana: Hidden or "closed" medicinal preparations believed to possess concentrated spiritual or physical power.</term> not only disciples (whether they be beginners or the unwise) but even the most knowledgeable Masters of the more secret Chemistry. Hence also his Recipes <note>original: "Recepta," referring to medical or chemical formulations.</note> were shortened by strange abbreviations; while they are truly learned to the learned, to us they seem as if mutilated and imperfect. Furthermore, they are so masked in the most secret terms of Adept Chemistry <term>Adept Chemistry: Also known as "Hermetic" or "Spagyric" chemistry, focusing on the spiritual and essential forces within matter rather than just its outward appearance.</term> that they deceive not only those of a dull wit <note>original: "duræ cervicis," literally "stiff-necked," a biblical idiom used here to mean those who are slow or stubborn in understanding.</note>, but even minds of a more subtle sharpness.

This impossibility of understanding (I might almost say) is increased by common recipes being intermixed with Paracelsian secrets; to distinguish one from the other is the task not of a student, but of a most highly practiced master.

Finally, that which was at once my first and greatest obstacle in these difficulties was my own [deficiency] concerning...

...[deficiency was] a certain unhappy preconception regarding the **Alkahest** <note>original: "Alkahest." A hypothetical universal solvent sought by alchemists, capable of dissolving every other substance.</note>. For, despairing of learning the preparation of this liquid from the books of others—or even from Paracelsus’s own book *On the Powers of the Limbs* <note>original: "de viribus membrorum." This work by Paracelsus discusses the medicinal properties of various substances in relation to the human body.</note>—I revisited the passages concerning the **lesser circulate** and the **specific corrosive** (since these are used as synonyms for the **Alkahest** by other authors).

To these I gradually added "Water" or "**Oil of Salt**" <term>Oil of Salt: Concentrated hydrochloric acid, often produced by distilling salt with clay or other additives.</term>, "**Corrosive Water**" <note>original: "Aquam Comedentem," literally "Eating Water," a term for a strong acid.</note>, "**Aqua Regis**" <term>Aqua Regis: "Royal Water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids named for its ability to dissolve "noble" metals like gold.</term>, the **greater circulate**, and others. I did this because I was fully convinced that a single **universal solvent** <term>menstruum: A solvent used in chemistry to extract or dissolve substances; a "universal" one was believed to be the key to the Great Work of alchemy.</term> was intended by all these names. My hope was that, even if I could not find the method for preparing this liquid in any one place, I might discover it by comparing all these various passages together. 

But the labors I endured as a result were manifold and hardly believable—yet they were entirely in vain and grueling. Conquered at last by these efforts and frustrated in all my hopes, I had intended to abandon **Chemistry** and **Medicine** altogether, viewing them as arts far beyond my own natural abilities. 

But look! Unexpectedly, the eyes of my mind were opened, and I saw

...all these things differed not only in name, but also in material, preparation, and use. Thus, in place of the one liquid I was seeking, the **Alkahest** <term>Alkahest: A hypothetical universal solvent sought by alchemists, believed to be capable of reducing any body to its first matter.</term>, I found in **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who revolutionized medicine by using chemicals and minerals.</note> many **solvents** <term>menstrua: In alchemy, liquids used to dissolve solids or extract their medicinal properties.</term>. I had already learned, following **Paracelsus**, how to prepare and distinguish the multiple medical uses of them all into **Essences** <term>Essentias: The refined, "spiritualized" core of a substance, purified of its dross.</term>, **Magisteries** <term>Magisteria: Preparations where the substance is transformed but retains its full medicinal power.</term>, **Stars** <term>Astra: The celestial or vital influences inherent in a physical substance.</term>, **Secrets** <term>Arcana: Hidden, highly potent medicinal virtues in nature.</term>, and those things he calls "lesser" **Medicines** <term>Medicamina: Basic medicinal preparations.</term>.

In this way, what was most difficult for others to understand in **Paracelsus** became clearer to me than all the rest; and so, I attained the end sooner than the beginning <note>The author suggests he mastered the complex classification of results (the "end") before he had truly mastered the foundational practical principles (the "beginning").</note>. However, the joy that grew from this was shorter than expected. For, after many experiments were tried in vain, I was taught that these Paracelsian **solvents** <term>menstrua</term> contain something secret and unknown within them, which was by no means to be understood literally. For that reason, I began to examine them more exactly; and while [comparing] their qualities with the nature of the **Alkahestic** <term>Alkahestici: Pertaining to the Alkahest, the universal solvent.</term> liquid...

When I compared them, I found the greatest difference between this [the Alkahest] and those others [the solvents]. 

For the liquid **Alkahest** <term>Alkahest: A hypothetical universal solvent sought by alchemists, famously described by Jan Baptist van Helmont as being able to reduce any matter to its primary liquid state without being consumed itself.</term> is said to be unique and universal; but the **solvents** <term>menstrua: From the Latin 'menstruum'; in alchemy, these are liquids used to dissolve solids or extract medicinal virtues.</term> of **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician who pioneered the use of minerals and chemicals in medicine.</note> are many. The former is indestructible; the latter are destructible. The former scorns any union with physical bodies <note>original: "corporum ſpernens connubium"</note>; the latter remain within them. The former preserves the natural powers of things; the latter alter them. The former rises during distillation after the **Essences** <term>Essentias: The refined, concentrated medicinal or spiritual core of a substance.</term> of things; the latter rise before their dissolved components, and so forth.

For a long time I wavered, unsure which side I should favor. At one moment, I desired for myself the one indestructible liquid rather than many destructible solvents, believing one thing to be better than many. At another moment, having changed my mind, I preferred the solvents that were sufficient for the manifold uses I had only just learned.

At last, truth won out, for it had already shown me that I could demonstrate most, if not all, Paracelsian medicines in the works of **Guido** <note>Guido de Montanor, an influential 14th or 15th-century alchemist often cited in later chemical texts.</note> and **Basil** <note>Basil Valentine, the legendary Benedictine monk whose writings on antimony and chemical salts were central to early modern chemistry.</note>; on the contrary, the **Secrets** <term>Arcana: From the Latin 'arcanum' (hidden/secret); in Paracelsian medicine, these are the most potent, hidden healing virtues extracted from nature.</term> of Paracelsus are commonly pro- <note>The text breaks here; the catchword indicates the full word is "prostituted" or "exposed to the public."</note>

<summary>The author distinguishes between the universal Alkahest and the various specialized solvents used by Paracelsus, weighing the theoretical perfection of the former against the practical utility of the latter. He concludes that Paracelsus’s chemical methods can be validated through the earlier works of Guido de Montanor and Basil Valentine.</summary>

...established <note>Continuing from the previous page's "Para..." this completes the word "constituta" (established or arranged).</note>, as if prepared with that liquid **Alkahest** <term>Alkahest: In alchemy, a theorized universal solvent capable of dissolving any substance into its primary matter.</term>, or a similar liquid, I saw more and more that they varied from the authentic sources; indeed, they were even contrary to them. ...[ing] <note>This completes the word "nothing" from the previous page.</note> you can allege many things, but give me leave to suggest this to you: namely, that a distinction must be made between the theoretical and practical books of the **Adepts** <term>Adepts: (Latin: *Adepti*) Alchemists who have allegedly achieved the "Great Work" and discovered the secrets of transmutation and the Elixir of Life.</term>. <meta>This page continues the discourse on the dangers of alchemical literature, likely excerpted from Denis Zachaire’s "Opuscule très-excellent de la vraye philosophie naturelle des métaulx" as it appears in the Theatrum Chemicum. *In order to lead the true seekers of this art away from common errors and onto the true path—lest they squander their resources and suffer the loss of their labor, name, and reputation by insisting on the false **Recipes** <term>Recipes: (Latin: *Receptis*) In this context, specific laboratory instructions or chemical formulas found in medieval and Renaissance books.</term> found in books such as those of **Geber**, **Rhazes**, **Albertus Magnus**, the **Path**, the **Light**, the **Canon of the Pandects**, **Demophontis**, the **Summa**, and other misleading men—I will first recount my own errors, etc. And on page 750, he continues thus:* The number of those whom it is useless to list is infinite, and there is a vast abundance of books written on this subject using metaphorical words and figures, so that they cannot easily be understood by anyone except the **sons of the art** <note>original: "filiis artis"; a traditional term for initiated alchemists who believed they possessed a God-given understanding of nature's secrets.</note>. Reading these books leads one away from the right path and into various errors rather than toward the goal; among this group are **Michael Scot**, **Arnaldus de Villa Nova**, **Raymond Lully**, **Jean de Meung**, **Hortulanus the Truth-teller**, and others.

I have categorized these **solvents** into **vegetable** and **mineral** types. This is not because the "vegetable" ones must be made only from plants, or the "mineral" ones only from minerals. Rather, any solvent that lacks a manifest <term>acid</term> <note>original: *acido*. In 17th-century chemistry, an "acid" was defined by its sharp, biting nature and its tendency to react violently with other substances.</note> and acts without boiling or agitation is called **vegetable**, even if it is composed of purely animal or mineral substances by means of the <term>Spirit of Philosophical Wine</term> <note>original: *spiritu Vini philosophici*. Conversely, a solvent becomes **mineral** as soon as a manifest acid is mixed with either the Spirit of Philosophical Wine or a vegetable solvent. Because of the added acidity, it then dissolves bodies violently and with <term>effervescence</term> <note>original: *effervescentia*; the bubbling and fizzing seen during a chemical reaction.</note>. 

I have further subdivided both categories into **simple** and **compound**. This is not to imply that the "simple" ones are made of fewer ingredients, but because they possess a simpler or lesser power. **Simple** solvents have less effect on tinting the bodies dissolved in them, whereas **compound** solvents tint them more deeply.

## 3. The Spirit of Wine of Paracelsus.

### Description from Chapter IX of the Third Book of *On the Long Life*, page 64.

Digest Wine poured into a <term>pelican</term> <note>A specialized glass vessel with two "arms" that allow distilled vapors to circulate back into the main body, promoting "maturation" of the substance.</note> in horse manure <note>Used as a source of gentle, steady heat for the digestion process.</note>, and do so continuously for a two-month period; you will see it become so thin and pure that it spontaneously draws out onto the surface a certain fatness, which is the **Spirit of Wine**. Furthermore, whatever is beneath this exists as <term>Phlegm</term> <note>In alchemy, "phlegm" refers to the watery, tasteless, and inactive residue left after the "spirit" has been extracted.</note> devoid of any nature of Wine. The fatness alone, however, enclosed in a vial and <term>digested</term> <note>Heated gently over a long period to chemically transform the substance.</note> by itself, is of the highest energy for a long life.

->*Guido used the following method, which differs little from the Paracelsian one.*<-

## 4. The Essence of Wine of Guido.

### Described on page 1 of the *Chemical Treasure*.

<margin>Recipe</margin> Take White Wine, or Red, which is better; distill it from a <term>B.</term> <note>Abbreviation for *Balneum Mariae* (Mary's Bath); a water bath used for gentle heating.</note> until the material remains at the consistency of honey. Divide this into two parts in a doubled <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the lower part of a distillation apparatus.</note>, mix it with the distilled liquor, and join them again; after a digestion of six weeks is completed, a **Green Oil** will float on top; separate this using a <term>tritorium</term> <note>A separating funnel or vessel used to decant or part liquids of different densities, such as oil from water.</note>.

## *From the recipes, we observe the following things worthy of note.*

1. *That the Red or White Wine is not the common variety, but the **Philosophical**; and that this unique substance is what is kept obscured in these four books, to be understood not according to the letter, but through **Analogy**; yet <term>Burning Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua ardens"; high-proof distilled alcohol.</note>, <term>Water of Life</term> <note>original: "Aqua Vitae"; a term for concentrated medicinal alcohol.</note>, **Spirit**, or **Essence** are the proper names of the Philosophical Wine.*

2. *That the Burning Water of the Philosophical Wine agrees in certain respects with the properties of common Spirit of Wine; namely, that in distilling, it precedes its <term>Phlegm</term> <note>original: "Phlegma"; the watery, inactive residue left after the alcohol has been distilled off.</note>. It is <term>rectified</term> <note>Purified through repeated distillation.</note>, like the common kind, from its Phlegm. Finally, the rectified spirit is recognized by burning a cloth, sugar, etc.* <note>A common historical test for purity: if a cloth soaked in the spirit burned away without the cloth itself catching fire, or if the spirit consumed a lump of sugar entirely, it was considered sufficiently "rectified."</note>

3. *That by <term>circulating</term> <note>The process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel, intended to "refine" the substance over time.</note> this Burning Water, it daily loses its humidity and sharpness, and is finally reduced into a floating **Oil**, which is the **Essence** and **Spirit** of the Philosophical Wine. But who has ever reduced common Spirit of Wine, or Water of Life, into an Oil by circulation alone? Who has ever reduced that Oil to dryness by continued circulation? So that it can be sublimated like a **volatile salt**, by means of a sufficiently strong fire, as **Isaac** <note>Likely referring to Isaac Hollandus, a 15th-century alchemist famous for his works on the "Vegetable Stone."</note> testifies he has experienced in the description of his **Vegetable Stone**, about which [we will treat] below in the Third Book.*

Second, *Because like Heaven, it receives the forms of all things.*

Just as the universal form (the **Macrocosmic Heaven**) <note>original: "Cœlum Macrocosmicum"; the "Great World" or the universe as a whole, which reflects the "microcosm" of the human body.</note> has a desire for every form, so the **Fifth Essence** <note>original: "quinta Essentia"; the most refined substance, beyond the four physical elements.</note> (**Philosophical Wine**) <note>original: "Vini Phil."</note> [is inclined] toward any <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexionem"; in medieval medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's health.</note>; from which it is clearly evident that the Fifth Essence of things is said to be of that temperament to which it is joined: if it is joined to hot things, it becomes hot; if to cold things, cold, etc. Therefore the Philosophers called this "Heaven," since just as Heaven influences us sometimes with heat, sometimes with moisture, etc., so the Fifth Essence acts within human bodies at the Artist's <note>The "Artist" refers to the Alchemist performing the work.</note> pleasure, etc. *Distinction 1 of the Book of the Essence.* <note>Referring to the *Liber de Secretis Naturae seu de Quinta Essentia*, a seminal alchemical text attributed to Ramon Llull.</note> To this "Heaven," we apply its "stars," which are Plants, Stones, and **Metals**, so that they may communicate life and health to us. *In the same place.* <note>original: "Ibidem"</note>

The Oily <note>original: "Unctuosus"</note> **Spirit of Philosophical Wine** extracts only the oily natural **Essences** of **Vegetables**, as we shall observe below in the *Book of Medicines*. These Essences—as well as other crude, expressed, or distilled oily substances from both the Animal and Vegetable kingdoms—are divided by this Spirit of Wine through simple **digestion** <term>digestion: the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat to break it down or refine it</term> into two distinct parts: two Oils or fats. One of these is the **Essence** of the thing, and the other is the **Body**. We have previously named the Essence prepared in this way the "secondary Spirit of Wine."

Both Essences—the one prepared by division and the one prepared by extraction—become one through a longer digestion with the aforementioned Spirit of Wine. For those things which are of one and the same purity and of a shared nature <note>original: "symbolicæ naturæ," referring to substances with matching elemental qualities that allow them to bond</note> are mixed easily and inseparably; thus, the Essence prepared by means of the Essence is joined to that same Essence.

And if we prolong the digestion further, eventually one of the two fats—namely the **Body**, which is less oily and has therefore been left behind until now—is received into that shared nature. But I have a rebuttal: namely, that Lull also "sharpened" <note>original: acuisse; meaning to increase the potency or corrosive strength</note> his Spirit of Wine <note>original: Vini Spiritum; concentrated alcohol or ethanol used as a solvent</note> with raw vegetable substances. This is easily proven from the Third Distinction of the *Book of Essence*, in the "Figure of Individuals" <note>a diagram or classification of specific starting materials</note> cited by him, where he lists the most closely related "individuals" that sharpen the Philosophical Spirit of Wine. These are: Red Wine, new Honey, Celandine, the flower of Rosemary, Mercury-herb <note>original: Mercurialis; likely the plant *Mercurialis annua*</note>, Red Lily, Tartar, human blood, and White Wine.

Why he chose these and no others, or why he chose only these, is not for me to answer. What we learn from this is that he recommended two of these individuals above the rest to us: Tartar and Honey. Regarding these, he says: "There are certain individuals in which the Mercury (*Vegetable*) has a somewhat free action; in Tartar it has only one free operation alone, and in Honey it has two. The artist must know this so that he may be made certain in this art and its primary truth."

He prefers Tartar, not for the sake of the Tartar itself but for the sake of the <term>Alkali: a caustic salt, specifically potassium carbonate, obtained by burning plant matter—in this case, wine lees</term> made from it. He dissolves this as the best of alkalis through <term>deliquium: the process of allowing a salt to absorb enough moisture from the air that it naturally dissolves into a liquid</term>. Once purified, he circulates <note>a process of continuous distillation in a closed vessel, symbolizing purification and refinement</note> it together with the Philosophical Spirit of Wine, according to the doctrine in the first Table of Individuals...

Indeed, some work with two of these, and some with all three. Some work with their own **Earth** <note>the solid residue remaining after distillation or calcination</note>, a method I dislike because in this way a coarse oiliness and heaviness are introduced.

Some have used **Vegetables** <note>plant matter</note>; such as the herbs, roots, flowers, and seeds known to you, which contain powerful <term>Mercuries</term> <note>the vital, volatile essence or "spirit" of a substance in alchemy</note> within them. For this reason, those who treated it in this manner increased its "vegetable" form rather than making it dissolutive.

Some have applied joined **Flowers** <note>likely "Flowers of Sulphur" or another sublimated substance</note> for the sharpening; this is the principal method and our own intention, which is found in the **Opening Alphabet** <note>original: *Alphabeto apertoriali*; a coded system of alchemical operations used by authors like Raymond Lully to organize their secrets</note>.

Some, being ignorant of the true way of sharpening this **B.**, spent much time in preparing various <term>waters</term> <note>liquid chemical agents or acids</note> before they could place any <term>body</term> <note>a solid metallic or mineral substance</note> into **B.**, just as happened to us in the beginning when we were seeking this <term>practice</term> <note>original: *praxin*; the hands-on laboratory application</note>—

*And so, Sal Ammoniac—dissolved either by the Phlegm of Philosophical Wine (that is, unrectified Burning Water <note>original: "Aqua ardente non rectificata"</note>) or by the Philosophical Wine itself, then crystallized and resolved through deliquium—is distilled either by itself or with newly added Spirit of Wine into the Water of Sal Ammoniac.*

However, we never observe these three signs in the use of **mineral Solvents**.*

*Thirdly: Whether the **Adepts** warn the worker to beware of the air or fumes during the **Operation**, or of poison in the use of the substance once it is prepared. Indeed, by means of a mineral **Solvent**, even **Pearls**, **Coral**, and even **Gold** and other **dry substances** that are otherwise most innocent, become the worst **Poisons**.*

## 27. The Lesser Circulate or the Water of the Circulated Salt of Paracelsus,

### *From Book 10 of the Archidoxis* <note>Paracelsus’s Archidoxis is a foundational 16th-century text on "arch-secrets" or the most potent chemical medicines.</note>

Then distill it through a **retort** <term>retortam: a glass vessel with a long, curved neck used for distilling substances that require high heat</term>. ### 28. The Sweet Spirit of Salt of Basil Valentine

<margin>℞ <note>Take</note></margin>
Take one part of the spirit of salt, most highly dephlegmated <term>dephlegmated: purified by removing the "phlegm" or watery, inactive portion through distillation</term>, and half a part of the best spirit of wine, also highly dephlegmated—or of the prepared "Sulfur of Wine" <note>The flammable, oily essence of wine</note> which I shall discuss below (the description of which we just encountered in the preceding sections). The vessel must be closed so that it cannot "breathe" <note>original: "ne respiret," meaning it must be airtight to prevent the escape of volatile vapors</note>. Two parts of this vessel should be full and the remainder empty. In this manner, it ought to be placed within **horse dung** <term>horse dung: a common alchemical heat source, used to provide a gentle, steady warmth for digestion and fermentation</term> to putrefy until the urine itself turns black, which usually happens within forty or fifty days.

But so that the urine may putrefy and blacken in a shorter space of time, we have held this as a secret and proven it by true experiment: by mixing and joining with the aforementioned urine a cup of **water of life** <term>water of life: "aqua vitae," or highly concentrated alcohol/spirit of wine</term> (*philosophical*) which has first been **rectified** <term>rectification: the process of purifying a liquid, typically through repeated distillations</term> as well as possible; this will accelerate the putrefaction.

Once the putrefaction is complete, place the urine in a **urinal** <note>original: "urinali," here referring to a specific shape of glass vessel</note> (*cucurbit* <term>cucurbit: the lower, gourd-shaped part of a still containing the liquid to be distilled</term>) with an **alembic** <term>alembic: the "cap" or lid of a still that channels vapors into a cooling tube</term> and a receiver, all very well sealed. Two parts of the vessel should be full and the third empty. Then, in a **bath** <note>a "balneum" or water bath, providing gentle, indirect heat</note> with a gentle fire, you shall distill one part out of three, or for as long as it produces "veins" <note>original: "venas," referring to the visible streaks of condensation or "striae" that appear inside the glass when volatile spirits are rising</note> in the cap. Once these veins have passed and vanished, remove the receiver, and you shall keep it very well sealed with the distilled water—which is its **mercury** <term>mercury: in this context, the "spirit" or the most volatile, active essence of the substance</term> (*spirit*)—in as cold a place as you can.

# Vegetable salt ammoniac through the shortcut of Lullius,
### *In the Newest Testament.*

Son, with God’s help, that **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur (naturae)"; in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of a substance</note> can be wonderfully shortened <note>original: "accurtari," meaning to simplify or accelerate the chemical process</note>, and the method is as follows. Take our **liquid pitch** <note>original: "picem nostram liquidam," the dark, resinous residue remaining after an initial distillation</note> (left behind after the removal of the **phlegm** <note>original: "phlegmatis," the watery, tasteless part of a distilled liquid</note>) and place it in a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the base of a still</term>, in a fire of the **third degree** <note>a moderate to high heat, often achieved with a sand bath</note>, and extract the oil until the earth remains dry and burnt. Son, **calcine** <term>calcine: to heat a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or ash</term> it as I have taught you, and purify the earth, and thus separate the salt from it. Upon that salt, provide a fourth part of the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritûs," the volatile, active essence of the substance</note> which is in the second water (already distilled from the pitch) and **digest** <term>digest: to apply gentle, continuous heat to a substance to mature or transform it</term> it as described above, afterward drawing off the moisture (which is superfluous, tasteless, and to be rejected). Repeatedly add a fourth part, digest, and dry it as before, until the earth is **pregnant** <note>original: "praegnans," meaning the solid matter has fully absorbed and saturated itself with the liquid spirit</note>. The sign will be that nothing more will distill off (of the aforementioned phlegm or moisture). **Sublimate** <term>sublimation: the process where a solid turns directly into a gas and then back into a solid, used here to purify the substance</term> it, and you shall have clean and pure vegetable sulfur, possessing the same virtue as the first. Son, I warn you with the fear of God not to reveal this most excellent shortcut to anyone.

### 31. Lull’s Circulated Vegetable Sky.
*From the Book on Vegetable Matter, in the fifth practice.* <note>Refers to the "Liber de materia vegetabili," a work often attributed to Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in alchemical history.</note>

### 35. Lully's Rectified Water of Life,

(181)

...of any acid. Fire, says *Ripley* <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490) was a famous English alchemist and canon of Bridlington; his works were fundamental to later English and European alchemy</note>, differs in many ways; for one is natural fire, another is unnatural, another is elemental, and another is fire against nature.

**Natural fire** is that which proceeds from the influence of the sun, the moon, and the stars, by which are generated the spirits of *burning waters* <note>original: "aquarum ardentium"; often referring to distilled spirits or alcohols used as solvents</note>, the essential vapors of minerals, and even the natural virtues of living things.

**Unnatural fire** is "accidental" fire, which is called **moist fire** artificially made by the philosophers. It is also called fire of the "first degree," which, through the simple tempering of heat, is called a **Bath** <note>original: "Balneum"; a water bath or Bain-marie</note>, a **stove**, or a **dung-bed** <note>original: "sterquilinium"; a pit of decomposing horse manure used to provide a steady, gentle heat for months at a time</note>; in this fire, the **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the stage of the "Great Work" where the matter decays, turns black, and "dies" before it can be reborn and purified</term> of our stone takes place.

**Elemental fire** is that which fixes, calcinates <note>to reduce a substance to powder through heat</note>, and burns, and it is nourished by combustible things.

**Fire against nature** dissolves potentially, wears down, kills, and destroys the governing power of the stone’s form: for it dissolves the stone into "water of the cloud" with the destruction of its specific form. It is called "fire against nature" because its operation is contrary to all natural operations, as *Raymond* <note>Raymond Lully (Ramon Llull), a 13th-century polymath to whom many influential alchemical treatises were attributed</note> asserts. For this fire destroys and leads to corruption everything that nature has composed, unless the "fire of nature" is added to it, etc. *The Marrow of Philosophy, page 135.* <note>original: "Med. phil. pag. 135"; referring to the "Medulla Philosophiae," a text often attributed to George Ripley</note> Wherefore and...

<margin>Recipe.</margin>
Take two parts each of calcined alum <term>alumen calcinatum; alum heated until it becomes a white, porous mass</term> and nitre <term>saltpeter</term>, and one part of roasted salt; mix them. Take one pound of this mixture and one pound of mercury sublimate <term>mercuric chloride, a highly toxic and volatile salt</term>; sublimate these according to the rules of the art. Mix the resulting sublimate with a fresh mixture of the salts and sublimate again; repeat this a third time. To this mercury, thus sublimated and pulverized, pour on philosophical spirit of wine <term>spiritus vini philosophici; a highly purified, concentrated alcohol</term>, which you must then draw off in a water bath <note>original: "balneo"</note> until it reaches an oily consistency. Cohobate <note>the process of pouring a distilled liquid back onto its residue to redistill it, concentrating its "virtue"</note> several times, and on the fourth time the mercury will ascend together with the spirit of wine. Rectify the distilled liquid until it leaves no dregs behind, and it will be a burning water <note>original: "aqua ardens"</note> like the Fire of Gehenna <note>original: "ignis Gehennæ"; Gehenna refers to a place of fire or hell, implying a solvent of extreme, "hellish" corrosive power</note>. Rectify this water further over an ash bath until it ascends leaving no residue; finally, distill it through sevenfold paper <note>a thick layer of filter paper</note> in a water bath, and you will have a truly spiritual water which you must keep in a very well-closed vessel because it is extremely volatile.

## 46. Mercurial water through the mastery of the three vessels of Lull,

...rightly corrected Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist often cited in Hermetic literature</note> with his long argument; yet if one considers the meaning of the words, there is nothing here deserving of correction. "Boiling water," the name of Arnold’s solvent <note>original: "menstrui," a liquid used in alchemy to dissolve or extract the essence of a solid</note>, is that supreme and almost unique secret which Arnold hid within the entire practical portion of his book; had he made it known, he would have exposed <note>original: "prostituisset," meaning to make common or debase</note> the whole of secret **Chemistry** <note><term>Chymia</term>: The art of alchemy, involving the transformation of matter</note>. That he did not mean common boiling water is proved by the following points:

1. Gold or silver must be dissolved into quicksilver or the **first matter** <note><term>prima materia</term>: The primitive, formless substance from which all things are created</note>, the **First Being** <note><term>primum Ens</term>: The fundamental essence or source-identity of a substance</note>, essence, etc., by means of quicksilver—not the common kind, but that which is philosophically prepared. Nothing reduces gold into its first matter except the first matter itself, just as here the first matter of common mercury is the **pure mercury** <note><term>mercurius mundus</term>: Purified mercury, stripped of its "earthy" dross</note> or the **mercury of mercury**. The adepts <note>Successful alchemists who have mastered the "Great Work"</note> have a rule: that first matter prepares first matter. Therefore, just as mercury prepares mercury, essence prepares essence, and mastery <note>original: "magisterium," a perfected alchemical substance or process</note> prepares mastery; so the **philosophers' mercury** <note><term>mercurius philosophorum</term>: A sophisticated alchemical reagent, distinct from the liquid metal found in nature</note> of gold <note>original: "solis," literally "of the sun"</note> or silver <note>original: "lunæ," literally "of the moon"</note>, or the **First Being**, Essence, etc., cannot be prepared except by the **philosophers' mercury**, the First Being or a specific Essence. For this reason, in this recipe, we understand "boiling water" to mean the essence of mercury, and by no means common hot water.

...because it did not naturally have **earth** <note>original: "terram"; in alchemical theory, 'earth' represents the solid, stabilizing principle that prevents a substance from evaporating or melting too easily</note> homogeneous to itself in its composition, as **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> does; which earth is indeed the cause of permanent **fixation** <term>Fixation<span>The alchemical process of making a volatile substance (one that vaporizes easily) stable and resistant to the heat of fire.</span></term> in homogeneous substances. If, therefore, mercury has acquired **transparency** <note>original: "diaphaneitatem"</note> during the **Work of the Philosophers** <note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>, it will by right remain an unrestrainable substance, nor will it be congealed upon **Laton** <term>Laton<span>Also known as Latona; this term refers to the "black" or base metallic body—often an alloy of copper or lead—that must be cleansed and "whitened" during the alchemical process.</span></term> into a metallic form, species, and proportion. For it does not carry its own congealing with it or within itself—as water carries earth—which earth, as has been said, is **mercurial**; and it is the first cause of **thickening**, **coagulation**, and **fixation** <note>original: "inspissationis, coagulationis, & fixionis"</note>.

If, then, this water remains thus outside of the metallic proportion, how can similar species be procreated from this composition? Thus, those people err who think they can extract clear, transparent water from mercury and perform many wonders with it. For even if they were to produce such a water, it would be of no use to the **Work**, nor to its nature or proportion, nor could it restore or build up a perfect metallic species. 1. *Solvents <term>menstrua<span>From the Latin 'menstruus' (monthly); these were liquids used to dissolve solids, often requiring a month-long digestion process.</span></term> can and ought to be prepared according to their intended uses. ### *Canon 43, Distinction 1, of the Book of the Quintessence.*

<margin>Take:</margin> The **water of mercury**, which should be prepared in the manner we have described in our *Testament* (the most recent one) and in the book titled *On Mercuries* <gloss>mercurial solvent, or the "glorious water" of common quicksilver, described above under number 44</gloss>. In this water, my son, dissolve half an ounce of the purest **silver** <note>original: "lunae." In the symbolic language of alchemy, Luna (the Moon) refers to silver, while Sol (the Sun) refers to gold.</note>. After the dissolution has been filtered, the water should be separated from the dregs <gloss>distill the solvent from the silver by means of an alembic</gloss>, in which the **viscosity of the silver** <note>original: "limositas argenti." This refers to the metallic "oil" or essence that is separated during distillation.</note> will rise. This water, my son, is a solvent for all other bodies and for quicksilver itself. By its power, my son, **pearls** are restored to their original nature in the manner we have described in our *Testament*, and in the *Compendium on the Testament and the Codicil* sent to **King Robert** <note>Robert of Anjou (1275–1343), King of Naples. Many alchemical works were dedicated to him, particularly those in the "pseudo-Lullian" tradition which combined alchemy with medical and spiritual reform.</note>.

The second water is made in this way. <margin>Take:</margin> Half an ounce of **lead**, and a sufficient amount of the aforementioned water. After you see that the lead has been dissolved, separate the water by filtered distillation <gloss>filter the solution of lead</gloss> and cast out the dregs, for they are of no value. ### From the Received Teachings we note:

1. That the **ethereal waters** are the essences of metals exposed to the influences of the Heavens for a year.

2. That the **terrestrial waters** are the bodies of the essences dissolved in their own **solvents** <note>original: "menstruis propriis." In alchemy, a 'menstruum' is a liquid used to dissolve a solid, named for its cyclical or "monthly" action.</note> and buried for a year.

of noble <note>Completing the word "nobilium" from the previous page</note> substances, both simple and composite, the Adepts have composed types by tempering the **philosophical spirit of wine’s** <note>original: "spiritûs vini phil."; high-grade ethanol used as a base solvent</note> oiliness with the manifold dryness of things. ->( 308 )<-

### Observations from the Recipes

1. We observe that the **Slimes** <note>original: "Limos"; refers to the viscous residues or precipitates formed during the breakdown of matter in a solvent</note> in their compositions are indeed clear, but they are (deliberately) veiled by complex, deceptive language and masked by such a great variety of operations—made further tedious by the long duration of time required—that they deter unprepared beginners.

2. These **Slimes** differ from the previously mentioned ethereal and terrestrial waters <note>the distilled liquids described on earlier pages</note> in the subtlety of their preparation; these are the elements of **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "salis harmoniaci"; ammonium chloride, a key reagent for dissolving metals</note> or the **philosophical mercury of the sun and moon** <note>original: "mercurii phil. solis & lunæ"; the refined "spirit" or liquid essence of gold and silver</note>; the former, however, are elements of raw metal. For **Lullius** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval philosophy to whom many alchemical works were later attributed</note> said: "Slimes intended for alchemical tinctures must be of a subtler nature than those intended for precious stones."

3. These **Slimes** are exalted essences, exposed to the influences of the heavens and the earth, and are therefore **medicines**.

4. In the same manner, the **sulfurs of nature** <note>the active, combustible principle of a substance</note> of imperfect metals <note>such as lead, tin, or copper</note> provide **Slimes** for nature that are just as strong in their own kind as the sulfurs of the nature of gold and silver are in theirs.

Thus far we have treated **vegetable solvents** <note>original: "menstruis vegetabilibus"; solvents derived from organic or plant-based matter, like wine or vinegar</note>; there now follow those which are called **mineral**. But before we proceed further, we must be warned that through vegetable <note>The text transitions here to discuss the limitations or specific uses of organic solvents compared to mineral ones</note>

### Annotationes. ###

Until now, we have blended the unctuous **philosophical spirit of wine** <term>spiritus vini philosophicus; a highly rectified and specialized alcohol used as a universal solvent in alchemy</term> with substances that are oily, dry-oily, oily-dry, or purely dry, and we have organized them into various classes of vegetable **solvents** <term>menstrua; liquids used to dissolve or extract the essence of a solid substance</term>. Among these, we have presented solvents that are in every way complete and perfect—incomparable in odor, taste, and color—which dissolve substances without noise or effervescence, and remain permanently combined with the materials they have dissolved. 

Next in order are those known as mineral solvents. Although these possess a foul odor, an acid or corrosive taste, and are most often milky and opaque in color—indeed, they dissolve bodies with the greatest violence and corrosion—nonetheless, because they have that same philosophical spirit of wine and the vegetable solvents as their basis, they are just as stable as the others. In fact, they are even better than the vegetable versions in terms of shortening the time required for the work.

For the added acidity of mineral salts (the reason why mineral solvents are called corrosive or acid) cannot destroy the nature of the spirit of wine, nor the nature of the vegetable solvents. Instead, by the process of corrosion, it makes the particles of dry substances more suitable for uniting them with the oily philosophical spirit of wine. But if indeed

**Adrop** is called **leprous gold**. <note>original: *aurum leprosum*. ### 63. Ripley’s Solvent of Sericon.

*Found in the Vade Mecum, commonly called the Bosom Book.*

<margin>Take:</margin> Thirty pounds of <term>Sericon <note>original: *Sericon*. In Ripley’s alchemy, this usually refers to "red lead" (minium), though it was sometimes associated with antimony.</note></term> or antimony, from which you will obtain about twenty pounds of "gum," provided that the vinegar is of good quality. Dissolve each pound of that Sericon in two measures (one gallon) of twice-distilled vinegar. ...of the nature of metals: which by some is named the calcining agent <note>original: calcantis; referring to vitriol or the substance that reduces metals to powder</note> and **glassy azoth** (*vitriolated mercury or azoquean vitriol*), which is the earth and the ore of metals. (358)

A great mystery of the art is revealed here by **Ripley** <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist and author of *The Compound of Alchymy*</note>; because of this disclosure, he fears not only the disapproval of the **Adepts** <term>Adepti; masters who have successfully achieved the Great Work of alchemy</term>, but most especially the displeasure of God. Indeed, the nature of our **green lion** <term>leo viridis; a symbol for the raw mineral matter or the acidic solvent used to "devour" metals</term>, what our **common mercury** is (which is more "common" to us than ordinary quicksilver), and what the **azoquean vitriol** <note>original: *vitriolum azoqueum*; likely a reference to a purified or "animated" vitriol, with "Azoc" being a term for mercury</note> and the **solvent** <term>menstruum; a powerful alchemical solvent</term> made from it are—these things **Lully** <note>Raymund Lully (c. 1232–1315), a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy</note> and others have revealed clearly enough to their students, though it might not seem so to those of us who are less instructed in the matter. 

However, Ripley testifies that concerning the present **Secret** <note>original: *Arcano*</note>, no one has ever spoken so plainly. The **Adepts** indeed handed down in their practical instructions the use of **(philosophical) wine** <note>original: *vini (philosophici)*; not common wine, but a highly distilled alchemical spirit or solvent</note> without the "cloak of philosophy" <note>i.e., without excessive metaphorical concealment</note>. Among them, **Raymund** and **Arnold** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a physician and alchemist</note>, along with certain others, attained the knowledge of it; yet (to use Ripley's expression in his *Medulla* <note>Referring to Ripley's work *Medulla Alchimiae*, or *The Marrow of Alchemy*</note>), they remained silent on how it might actually be obtained. 

For this reason, while they were silent, Ripley is the first and only one to declare to us that the key of the entire **secret Chemistry** <note>original: *secretioris Chymiæ*</note> lies there—namely, in the **milk and blood of the green lion**. That is to say: the **stinking solvent** <term>menstruum fœtens; the foul-smelling liquid produced during the initial stages of the work</term> (or its component parts, the **mercury** and **sulfur**, the **Virgin’s Milk**, and the **lion’s blood**, the **white and red mercury**) [must be] **digested** <term>digerere; to subject a substance to gentle, continuous heat, similar to incubation</term> for fourteen days...

**Lully’s** rectified Water of Life is made through various **cohobations** <term>cohobatio; the process of repeatedly distilling a liquid from its own solid remains to concentrate its "virtue"</term> over its own **dead head** <term>caput mortuum; the useless solid residue left over after all liquids have been distilled away</term>. We are free to proceed by another way or method. Distill the stinking solvent after it has been **digested** <note>original: *digestum*; kept at a gentle, steady heat to encourage chemical breakdown</note> for 14 days; first, the **Burning Water** <note>original: *Aqua ardens*; a flammable spirit, typically alcohol</note> will rise, then the **phlegm** <note>original: *phlegma*; the watery, inactive portion of a distillate</note>, and in the bottom remains a thick material, like melted pitch. These are the constitutive principles of all vegetable solvents.

Let us therefore cease from further pursuit of the said **green lion**, whom we have chased through the meadows and the **forest of Diana** <note>The "Forest of Diana" is a metaphorical landscape representing the early stages of purification, often associated with silver or the moon</note>, along the **path of Saturn** <note>original: *viam saturni (philos.)*; "philosophical Saturn" refers to the heavy, dark stage of the work, often associated with lead or the *nigredo* (blackening) phase</note>, all the way to the **philosophical vineyards**. This present place, most pleasant, is given to the disciples of the art so that, after such great labors and sweats, and dangers to fortune and life, they may here refresh themselves, performing **women's work and children's play** <term>opera mulierum & lusus puerorum; a famous alchemical aphorism meaning that the final stage of the work is easy and requires only gentle, patient heat, much like household tasks</term>, content with the lion...

Thus **Ripley** (in his discussion on the **solvent** <note>original: *menstruo*; a powerful solvent used to dissolve metals</note> under No. 61) says: "You shall receive the blood..."

### 65. Paracelsus’s Green Lion
->*The Golden Fleece (German edition), p. 41.*<-

<margin>Recipe</margin> Take distilled vinegar, in which you must dissolve the **green lion** <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "Green Lion" often refers to vitriol (acidic minerals) or the raw, unrefined matter of the Great Work</note>; place it in putrefaction <note>a period of "decaying" or fermenting the substance in a warm environment</note>, filter the solution, and draw off the wateriness in a water bath <note>original: *B.*, short for *Balneum Mariae*, a gentle double-boiler method</note> until it reaches an oily consistency. Place this oil or residue in a retort and distill the moisture over a sand bath with a gentle fire. Then increase the fire, and the **green lion**, forced by the power of the fire, will give up its **Glue** <note>original: *Gluten*; a sticky or essential substance</note>, otherwise called air. To the <term>dead head</term> <note>original: *capiti mortuo*; the useless solid residue remaining after distillation</note> pour back its phlegm (*the moisture that was drawn off*); let it putrefy in dung <note>horse dung was used as a natural, steady source of low heat</note> (or a water bath) and distill it as before, and the spirits will rise again. Press more strongly with the heat, and a sticky oil of a lemon-yellow color will come forth. Over the <term>dead head</term> pour the first distilled water once more, set it to putrefy, filter, and distill as you did before; finally, using a very strong open fire, a blood-red oil will emerge, which is elsewhere called "fire." Burn the remaining earth <note>original: *reverbera*; to heat a substance in a reverberatory furnace</note> until it reaches whiteness, etc.

### From the Received Teachings we observe.

1. *Solvents* <term>menstrua: powerful liquid agents used to dissolve and transform matter</term> *of this kind are the first of all others, both mineral and vegetable, being prepared from the very matter of the **philosophical wine** or the **philosophical grapes**.*

2. *The milky liquor or spirit, **virgin’s milk** <note>original: "lac virginis"</note>, **white mercury**, Lully’s **white wine** <note>referring to the influential alchemical writings attributed to Ramon Lull</note>, and the **glue of the green lion** <note>original: "gluten leonis viridis"</note> are synonyms. Elsewhere, this is called the **glue of the eagle** by Paracelsus. Conversely, the **red liquor**, the **blood of the green lion**, **red mercury**, the **sulfur of the Philosophers**, and Lully’s **red wine** are likewise synonyms—which Paracelsus calls the **blood of the red lion**.*

3. *Acidic mineral solvents, through digestion or further refinement, are transmuted either into a simple vegetable solvent or into the **heaven** or spirit of the philosophical wine.*

4. *These acidic solvents must be distilled with the utmost caution because of the excessive power of the **azoquean vitriol** <note>vitriol associated with "Azoth" or mercury, known for its volatile and corrosive nature</note> or...*

71. Water or oil of salt of Paracelsus,
*Chapter 3, Book X of the Archidoxes, page 38.*
<note>The "Archidoxes" (Archidoxa) is one of the most influential works by Paracelsus (1493–1541), focusing on the extraction of "mysteries" or essences from matter.</note>

Although there are many ways to extract the **First Essence** <term>Ens primum: the "First Being" or most primordial, vital essence of a substance, believed to possess powerful healing properties</term> of salt, this method—the process of making **circulated salt** <note>salt that has undergone "circulation," a process of continuous distillation and condensation in a sealed vessel to refine it</note>, the lesser circulation from salt, the solvent water, or the water or spirit of circulated salt described above under No. 27—is nevertheless the most useful and efficient. After this, there is that other way, which we mentioned regarding the **Elixir of Salt**. Namely, that fresh salt mixed with the solvent water (which is the distilled spirit of circulated salt) should be putrefied and distilled for so long until the entire substance of the salt is dissolved and reduced into a permanent oiliness, with the body of the **phlegm** <term>phlegma: in early chemistry, the watery, tasteless, and inactive part of a substance that remains after distillation</term> removed from it in this manner. In this same way, the instruction is given for preparing the **Secret** <term>Arcanum: a "great mystery" or a concentrated medicinal essence that acts directly on the body’s vital force</term> or the mastery of **Vitriol** <note>sulfate minerals, often iron or copper sulfate</note> and **Tartar** <note>potassium bitartrate, the crust that forms in wine barrels, highly valued in alchemy</note>, as with all other salts.

*We have noted that the solvents <term>menstrua: alchemical solvents used to dissolve solids or extract essences</term> of the preceding category are prepared from the oily matter of the philosophers' wine <note>original: "vini phil."; refers to the "spirit of wine" or highly rectified ethanol used as a base in many alchemical processes</note>, purified, dissolved, and volatilized by acid; in the present category, we will observe the opposite: namely, that the acid or saline essences of salts, prepared with the oily spirit of the philosophers' wine, are the solvents of this fourteenth category.* Paracelsus, *in the prescribed recipe, reduced salts into a liquid substance or oil by the water of circulated salt <note>salt that has been purified through repeated distillation</note> through cohobation <term>cohobation: the process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto its solid residue and re-distilling it to concentrate the essence</term> alone. *In the "Key to the Archidoxis," specifically in Book 10, page 37, Paracelsus described the Essences of salts in these words:*

> The extraction of the <term>Quintessence</term> from salts—such as <term>Vitriol</term> <note>Iron or copper sulfates.</note>, Salt, <term>Nitre</term> <note>Saltpeter or potassium nitrate.</note>, <term>Tartar</term> <note>Potassium bitartrate, found in wine barrels.</note>, and so on—is done in this way. <term>Cohobate</term> <note>A process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto the solid material it was distilled from to further extract its "spirit."</note> it frequently with its own liquor or Water; <term>putrefy</term> <note>To digest or age a substance in gentle heat, often using a warm water bath or dung, to break it down.</note> it with the <term>phlegm</term> <note>The tasteless, watery distillate that lacks the active medicinal "spirit" of the substance.</note>, and from there withdraw the body in the manner of phlegm until you reach the <term>fixed spirit</term> <note>The part of the substance that resists the heat of the fire and remains at the bottom of the vessel.</note>. Dissolve this in its own Water or "wave" and, in heat, separate the pure from the impure using <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>Alcohol, usually highly distilled brandy or wine.</note>.

*This description is highly obscure, but it is rendered clearer by what has just been stated. the permanence of the rite <note>In this context, "rite" refers to the established alchemical procedure or the natural order of the operation.</note>, namely insofar as these **solvents** <term>original: "menstrua"; in alchemy, a solvent capable of dissolving solids, named from the idea of a cycle or "month."</term> are oily and mixed with dry substances, being very little diluted by their own wateriness; for all these watery parts separate themselves during **fixation** <term>The process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat, so it no longer evaporates.</term> as if they were useless. **Fifth**, regarding **mineral solvents** <term>original: *menstrua mineralia*; inorganic acids or chemical solutions used to dissolve minerals and metals.</term>, you will note this: that their acidity has the same relationship as the **phlegm** <term>original: *phlegmate*; in alchemy, the watery, tasteless, and inactive part of a substance remaining after distillation.</term> or wateriness of vegetable solvents, insofar as it is moist, and therefore must be separated during the **fixations** <term>The process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</term> of things.

Insofar as it consists of dry particles of **mineral salts** (for dry salts are dissolved by acids), it falls under a twofold consideration.

In the first: if the acidity of the solvent happens to exist in a greater quantity than necessary, or if it adheres around the surface of the dissolved substance, it is easily washed away with common water.

In the second, however: if that same acidity is more skillfully mixed and absorbed by the dryness of the dissolved substance, it becomes the cause of **toxicity** <note>original: *venenositatis*; often referring to the corrosive or harmful "stinging" quality of a mineral that must be removed for medicinal use.</note>, and it can now only be altered by vegetable solvents that transmute it. **Paracelsus** does not command us to wash away the **oil of salt** <note>original: *salis oleum*; usually referring to a concentrated, purified form of salt or hydrochloric acid.</note>, but rather the **sharpness of salt** <note>original: *salis acredinem*.</note>, which does not penetrate into the substance of the metal and is easily removed by washing; however, the oiliness <insert>of salt...</insert>

"Various ways," he says in Book 4 of the **Archidoxis regarding the Essence** <note>original: *Archid. de Essentia*; refers to one of Paracelsus's most influential works, *Archidoxis magicae*, which details the preparation of chemical medicines.</note>, page 12, "are found through which the **Quintessence** <term>original: *Essentia quinta*; the "fifth essence," representing the purest, most potent medicinal core of a substance, stripped of its physical impurities.</term> can be extracted: namely through **sublimation** <term>Turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it.</term>, **calcination** <term>Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder.</term>, through **strong waters** <term>original: *aquas fortes*; mineral acids like nitric acid.</term>, through corrosives, through sweet things, through bitter things, etc., by whatever way it can be done. Wherein this must be simultaneously cared for: that everything which was added to the Quintessence out of the necessity of extraction must itself be extracted again, and so the Quintessence remains alone, contaminated or mixed with no other things. For it cannot happen that from metals, and especially from gold—which cannot be overcome by itself—the Quintessence is extracted unless some suitable corrosive is applied, which can afterwards be separated from it again. Thus salt which was dissolved in water is extracted from the water again, so that the water lacks salt. Where, however, this..."

( 399 )

...must be considered; namely, that not every **corrosive** <term>original: *corrosivum*; a sharp, acidic solvent used to break down materials</term> is suitable for this purpose, because not all of them can be [easily] separated. For if **Vitriol** <term>original: *Vitriolum*; metallic sulfates, typically of iron or copper, used in alchemical acids</term> or **Alum** <term>original: *Alumen*; a mineral salt used as an astringent and solvent</term> is mixed with water, neither can be separated from it afterward without damage or corruption; they will inevitably leave a harsh residue behind. This occurs because both substances are "watery" in nature, and thus these two likes run together—which is exactly what should be avoided in this process.

Therefore, we must take care: we should not apply watery to watery, or oily (*unctuous*) to oily, nor resinous to resinous. Instead, a **contrary** substance must separate and extract the **Quintessence** <term>original: *quintam Essentiam*; the "fifth essence," representing the purest, most medicinal core of a substance</term>. For example, "waters" (aqueous solvents) extract the Quintessences of oily things—as is taught regarding the treatment of metals—and oily substances extract the Quintessences of watery things, as we can learn from the Quintessences of herbs.

Once the Quintessence has been separated and extracted, the **corrosives** must then be separated once more; this task will be easy to accomplish. For oil and water are separated from one another with ease. However, oil cannot be extracted from oil, nor can water be extracted from water, without some inter-mixing. If such a residue were left in the Quintessence, it could cause the greatest harm. For it is necessary that the Quintessence be clear—

Second, an *Essence* is defiled when the **solvent** <term>original: *menstruum*; a liquid used to dissolve or extract materials</term> or *Essence* is used in a greater quantity than is appropriate for the extraction of another *Essence*. By this excess quantity, the quality of the *said Essence* is diluted, diminished, and, as it were, defiled; for this reason, the superfluity of the solvent must always be removed so that the *Essence* remains by itself alone, without any mixture.

Third, an *Essence* is defiled in its extraction with acidic or mineral solvents, according to the processes of the ancients. For an acid, even if it cannot be intimately mixed with any *Essence* (because the acid itself is not an *Essence*), is nevertheless easily absorbed or hidden by the dryness of mineral *Essences*. Thus, it becomes joined to the *said Essences* by accident, and from a substance that is otherwise harmless, it produces a most powerful poison. Therefore, so that the ancients might remove this, they first washed away what adhered externally to the body with a water bath; then, that which had been more deeply admitted, they transmuted by the action of vegetable solvents through dige- <note>The text cuts off at the catchword "dige-", likely referring to "digestion," a process of gentle, prolonged heating to extract or mature a substance.</note>

We believe that Paracelsus’s statement should be applied to this method, since he specifically dealt with it there, especially when he said that the oily **Essences** of metals should be extracted with aqueous solvents (that is, acidic or corrosive ones), while the **Essences** of herbs—which are "aqueous," or less oily in comparison to metals—should be prepared with oily solvents (that is, vegetable-based **solvents**). IN the preceding category, the philosophical spirit of wine <term>spirit of wine: high-proof alcohol or its alchemical essence</term> was dissolved in acids. 5. For those well-versed in the more secret **Chemistry**, it is very difficult to go astray. Indeed, anyone who understands the practice of this art will easily explain the recipe of any **Adept** <term>Adept: a master alchemist who has successfully discovered the "Philosopher's Stone" or reached the highest level of chemical knowledge.</term>, even if it is very obscure—whether from its intended use, its title, or the method of preparation itself. For it is almost impossible that one would not draw some light or sufficient direction from one or another of these three points to find the same recipe explained more clearly in the writings of that same or another **Adept**. **And** although recipes sometimes occur which seem similar to the recipes of common **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chymiæ vulgaris." This distinguishes laboratory chemistry focused on practical crafts from the "secret" or philosophical alchemy.</note> in their title, method of preparation, and use, the student of our art will nevertheless easily judge whether to approve or reject these recipes. *The quality of a good **solvent** <term>menstruum: a solvent, often derived from alcohol or acids, used to extract the essential properties of a substance.</term> is such that it dissolves bodies either gently or violently, and renders them not only volatile but also oily; indeed, it reduces them into a true oil that either floats upon or sinks beneath watery liquids. This attribute of a solvent belongs to no common dissolvent, but only to the philosophical ones, which are prepared from the oily **spirit of philosophical wine** <note>original: "spiritu vini phil." Likely refers to highly rectified ethanol used as a base for alchemical operations.</note>. This spirit alone, by its own permanence, renders the dry **sulfur** <term>sulfur: in alchemy, this refers to the "soul" or the flammable, active principle of a metal rather than the chemical element S.</term> of a metal both thinner and oilier. Therefore, whatever solvent promises such things in its use—things which cannot be achieved by common means—declare it to be philosophical, provided that one or two cautions are observed:*

1. *That the recipe be from some known and non-suspect author, and not from any **smoke-seller** <note>original: "fumivenduli." A historical term for a charlatan or a "seller of hot air" who makes grand promises without substance.</note> who promises great and many things without a foundation. Therefore, we believe that any recipe lacking its own authority, however plausible it may seem, should be rejected as suspect.*

2. *That the recipe not be solitary, but described by the same author in various places rather than just one, or at least be very clear in its ingredients. For the same names have one meaning for this **Adept** <term>Adept: a master of alchemy who has achieved the Great Work.</term> and another meaning for another; therefore, as long as [it is compared] through parallel*

The name **Sallabrum** <term>Sallabrum: an alchemical term derived from the Latin "sal" (salt) and "labrum" (basin or lip)</term> is said to be, as it were, a **basin of salt** <note>original: "salis labrum"</note>, not because salt is to be contained in this basin—just as a **candelabrum** is so named because candles are fixed in it—but rather because in this saline basin, the Essence of the fire of some metal, or some chemical light, is either to be preserved or prepared; just as **Alum** is called a **Lamp** <note>original: "Lucerna"</note> by Isaac in the *Hand of the Philosophers*, page 28.

Concerning this basin of salt, Thomas Aquinas <note>Many alchemical texts were historically attributed to the famous theologian Thomas Aquinas, though most are now considered pseudonymous</note> in the *Blessed Lily* <note>original: "Lilio Benedicto"</note>, page 1085, Volume 4 of the *Theatrum Chemicum* <note>A massive and influential compendium of alchemical writings published in the 17th century</note>, writes as follows:

> Add the basin of salt, as much as a sixth part of the two;
> Join them and place them together—

In the same place, he calls this basin of salt a medium for joining **Tinctures** <term>Tincturas: in alchemy, these are potent substances or "elixirs" capable of transforming the properties of metals or healing the body</term>. It is a medium between two extremes: between the hard and the soft, between the **moon** <note>the "moon" or "luna" is the alchemical symbol for silver</note> and the spirit, and between the body and the spirit. Just as menstrual blood is the medium between the seed of the male and the female, so is this salt of ours. On page 1085, he calls the Sallabrum "thundering salt," the "illuminating stone," and the **fat of the eagle** <term>pinguedinem aquilæ: a symbolic term often referring to the "oil" or concentrated essence of Sal Ammoniac (ammonium chloride)</term>. On page 1087, he calls it **Sal Alembrot** <term>Sal Alembrot: a double salt of mercury and ammonium chloride, highly valued by alchemists as a "universal solvent"</term>, the stone of Bore (Borax), and the fat of the eagle. On page 1097, he identifies it as **Tincar** <note>an old term for crude Borax</note> or Borax.

Nitre and common salt, fused together and dissolved through **deliquescence** <term>deliquium: the process where a substance absorbs moisture from the air until it dissolves into a liquid</term>, sometimes satisfied Paracelsus. Nor does the mystery of the recipe lie in the **Wax** <note>original: "Cera"</note>; if you choose another substance in its place, you will not err at all. In its place, he sometimes used **linseed oil** in water of the sixth gradation, but more on this in what follows.*

2. These **solvents** <term>menstrua: alchemical solvents used to dissolve solid matter</term>, by reason of their acidity, are both produced more quickly and work more powerfully than the aforementioned solvents of the fifth kind.

3. They are not always composed from the **philosophical spirit of wine** <note>original: "vini phil. spiritu"; highly distilled alcohol or a specialized alchemical substance believed to hold the "soul" of the wine</note>, but can also be made by means of some common oily substance, provided it is attempted by an artist experienced in the method of the philosophical spirit of wine.

4. These solvents, without any addition of **common quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi vulgi"; ordinary liquid mercury</note>, but by their own inherent powers, reduce metals and minerals into **running mercury**.

5. Metals dissolved and sublimated by these solvents are quite properly called the **mercuries of the philosophers**, because just like common **sublimated mercury** <note>mercury chloride</note>, these are very easily restored into running quicksilver.

## 89. The Bath of King Basil,
*From the Book of Particulars, in the Section on Gold.* <note>original: "Libr. Partic. in Particul. Solis." In alchemy, "Solis" (of the Sun) is the standard code for gold.</note>

<margin>Take:</margin> One part of saltpeter <term>saltpeter: potassium nitrate, a mineral salt used to create strong acids</term>, one part of sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used to make solvents more aggressive</term>, and half a part of powdered flint; mix these and distill them. Note: This water must be distilled with caution and precision, for it cannot be distilled by the common method; one experienced in the (more secret) operations of chemistry will know what must be done. Note: It is necessary that you have a strong earthenware retort <term>retort: a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</term> that is well-sealed with lute <term>lute: a clay or paste used to seal alchemical joints against heat and escaping vapors</term>. In the upper part of the retort, there should be a pipe half a span <note>A "span" is roughly 9 inches; half a span is about 4.5 inches.</note> long and two fingers wide. Attach a large receiver vessel, seal the joints well, and increase the fire by degrees until the retort glows white-hot. 

Then, through the pipe, throw in a spoonful of this mixture, and suddenly close the pipe with a damp cloth; the spirit <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the acidic vapors or gases produced by the reaction.</note> will pass impetuously into the receiver. Once the spirits have settled, throw in another spoonful of the said material, proceeding in this way until no material remains. You will then have a **Gehennean Water** <note>original: "Aquam Gehenneam." Referring to Gehenna, a place of fire or hell, signifying an extremely corrosive or "hellish" acid.</note>, which dissolves the calx <term>calx: the powdery residue left after a metal has been roasted or chemically broken down</term> of gold in an instant into a thick solution. I have mentioned this solution in the third part, as well as in the second key; it not only dissolves gold but also renders it volatile <term>volatile: in alchemy, this describes a solid substance that has been transformed into a gas or a liquid that can be easily evaporated</term>, etc.
