## 88. Ripley's Aqua Regis,
<note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490) was a famous English alchemist. "Aqua Regis" or "Royal Water" is a mixture of acids capable of dissolving gold, the "king" of metals.</note>
->*Page 349 of the Viaticum.*<-
<note>The "Viaticum" (The Wayfarer’s Manual) was one of Ripley's most influential alchemical works.</note>

Make a corrosive water <term>corrosive water: a powerful acid solvent</term> from saltpeter <term>saltpeter: potassium nitrate</term> and sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used to make acids more aggressive</term>, and do not put more than four ounces into the distilling vessel. Draw the water off with a gentle fire, in which you are to dissolve and make the **oil of gold** <note>original: "oleum solis." In alchemy, "Sol" (the Sun) is the code for gold; its "oil" is a liquid form of the metal.</note>, etc.

*This "strong water" <term>strong water: aqua fortis</term> was called the **King's Bath** by Basil Valentine, about which he writes the following in his "Explanation of the Second Key":* Note, friend, and consider seriously, for the principal secret lies hidden here. See to it that the Bath is prepared, and take care that no foreign substance enters it, lest the noble seed of gold be destroyed at its roots after its dissolution. Therefore, examine exactly and with caution the materials of which the Second Key informs you; namely, what materials are to be taken for the King's Bath, in which the King must be dissolved and his outward form broken so that his spotless soul may emerge. The **Dragon** and the **Eagle** serve this purpose—that is, saltpeter and sal ammoniac—from whose union "strong water" is made, as you will be instructed in my manuals where I shall treat the "particulars of gold" <note>original: "particulari solis." Alchemists used the term "particulars" to describe specific recipes for working with a single metal.</note>.

### 89. The Bath of King Basil,
->From the Special Book, regarding the Particulars of Gold.<-
<note>original: "Solis" (Sun), the alchemical code for Gold. A "Particular" operation usually refers to a specific transformation of a metal rather than the "Universal" Great Work.</note>

Take: one part saltpeter <term>saltpeter: potassium nitrate</term>, one part sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride</term>, and half a part of powdered flints; mix and distill. **Note:** This water must be distilled with caution and precision, for it cannot be distilled by the common method; one experienced in the operations of *more secret* chemistry <note>original: "chymiæ secretioris." This refers to advanced alchemy beyond standard apothecary work.</note> will know what must be done. **Note:** It is necessary that you have a strong earthen retort <term>retort: a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</term> well-sealed with clay <term>lutatam: sealed with "lute," a paste used to make joints airtight</term>, in the upper part of which a pipe emerges half a span <note>about 4-5 inches</note> long and two fingers wide. I made mention of this in the third part, as well as in the "Second Key"; it not only dissolves gold but reduces the same metal into a state of volatility <term>volatility: the ability of a substance to evaporate or be carried over in distillation</term>, etc.

### 90. *Philosophical water for the solution of Basil’s Gold,*

*From the first labor of the "Revelation of Manual Operations."*

<margin>Take:</margin> Two parts each of saltpeter <term>saltpeter: potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in energetic chemical reactions</term> and sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used here to provide chlorine for the solvent</term>, and one part of washed small stones <note>often flint or pebbles, used to distribute heat and prevent the mixture from foaming over</note>. Grind them together and distill the water through a tubulated retort <term>tubulated retort: a distillation vessel with a small opening or "pipe" at the top, allowing the chemist to add materials without dismantling the apparatus</term> into a large receiver, throwing in two or three ounces through the tube. The receiver must be large and should lie in a vessel full of cold water, and be covered with wet linen cloths so that the spirits may cool, for it will become extremely hot. Seal the joints of the retort very well, light the fire, and once the retort is heated, throw in three ounces of the material. With the tube immediately sealed, the spirits will pass over, the receiver will turn white <note>a sign of the "fuming" vapors of the acid</note>, and drops will fall. When the spirits have settled, throw in another three ounces, immediately sealing the tube; proceed as before, frequently changing the wet cloths. Continue this labor until you have enough water, which you should seal very well so it does not evaporate. This is the true water and the mineral Bath for the King <note>original: "Balneum minerale pro Rege." In alchemy, the "King" is the symbol for Gold; this "bath" is a solvent (Aqua Regia) capable of "dissolving" the king.</note>.

### 91. Paracelsus’s strongest Aqua Fortis, from Book 3 of the *Archidoxa* on the Separation of Elements, page 7.

<margin>Take:</margin> **Nitre** <term>Nitre: saltpetre (potassium nitrate), a key ingredient in explosives and strong acids</term>, **Vitriol** <term>Vitriol: a sulfate mineral used to create sulfuric acid</term>, and **Alum** <term>Alum: a chemical compound, usually potassium aluminum sulfate, used as a fixative and in purifying water</term> in equal parts. Distill these into an aqua fortis; pour this back again onto its dregs <note>original: "faeces," the solid residue left after distillation</note>, and distill it once more in a glass vessel. In this aqua fortis, clarify silver, and afterward dissolve sal ammoniac within it.

*It is demonstrated that Paracelsus did not mean the common variety of **sal ammoniac**, as shown by the use of the **menstruum** <term>menstruum: a solvent used to extract or dissolve metals and minerals</term>, which he describes thus: Having completed these steps, take the metal reduced into thin sheets and dissolve it in the water in that same place—that is, in the same water. Finally, separate it by means of a **Water Bath** <term>Water Bath: "Balneum Mariae," a method of heating a vessel by placing it in boiling water to ensure gentle, even heat</term>, and pour it on again. Repeat this as many times as necessary until an **oil** <term>oil: in alchemy, a liquid essence or "sulfur" of a metal, regarded as its most potent and medicinal form</term> is found at the bottom: chestnut-colored from **the Sun or gold** <note>original: "ex sole vel auro"</note>; azure from **the Moon** <note>original: "ex luna," referring to silver</note>; and red and very dark from **Mars** <note>original: "ex marte," referring to iron</note>;*

### 92. Guido’s Aqua Regis,

## 94. Lully’s Spirit of Vitriol mixed with Spirit of Wine,

->*The Abridged Epistle <note>original: "Epist. accurtatoria"; likely referring to the pseudo-Lullian work 'Epistola de Accurtatione,' a text focused on speeding up the alchemical process</note>, page 327.*<-

**Spirit of Vitriol** <term>spiritus vitrioli: sulfuric acid, traditionally produced by the distillation of "green vitriol" (iron sulfate)</term> is drier and coarser than the **spirit of the fifth essence of burning water** <term>spiritus quintæ Essentiæ aquæ ardentis: a highly refined and distilled alcohol, often compared to the "soul" of wine</term>, and there is a great harmony between the spirit of Vitriol and the nature of **Gold**, because both draw their origin from the same principles within the mineral kingdom. ### 97. The Water of the Sixth Gradation of Paracelsus,

### We note from the Recipes.

1. *That common **spirit of Vitriol** <term>spirit of vitriol: a strong acid, typically sulfuric acid, derived from minerals</term>, **butter of antimony** <term>butter of antimony: antimony trichloride, a thick, oily substance used in alchemical operations</term>, [the same of] arsenic, tin, etc., when mixed with the **philosophical spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritu vini phil." A highly refined or alchemically potent alcohol believed to act as a universal carrier.</note>, are actually the philosophical spirit of Vitriol, the philosophical butter of antimony, and so forth.*

2. *That **menstrua** <term>menstruum: a solvent used to dissolve or extract the essence of a substance</term> of this kind are the same as the menstrua of the fifteenth kind, yet with this distinction: in the latter, a non-tinting **philosophical vinegar** <note>original: "Acetum philosophicum." Not literal vinegar, but an alchemical solvent with acidic properties.</note> is produced; but in the present case, a tinting philosophical vinegar is prepared. This is because these [the present ones] are made from the acidic spirits of "tinting" things—that is, metals and minerals—whereas those [the fifteenth kind] are made from the acidic spirits of non-tinting things—that is, vegetable salts and certain minerals whose dry form was neither metal nor any colored body.*

3. *That these menstrua are not merely dissolving waters, but are at the same time **gradatory** <term>gradatory: a substance that increases the purity, color, or value of a metal</term>, because they are prepared from tinting substances.*

4. *That these menstrua are the **Essences** or **magisteries** <term>magistery: a medicinal preparation where the raw material is purified and concentrated into a potent form</term> of tinting things dissolved in acid, and are therefore medicines.*

5. *That these menstrua can also be made from crude oils, provided one knows the method of preparing the philosophical spirit of wine.*

6. *That these same two **oils of sulfur** <note>original: "sulphuris olea." Concentrated liquids derived from sulfur, valued for their supposed transformative powers.</note> (of which the red...*

### Annotations.

*The preceding category contained mineral <term>solvents: the original text uses "menstrua," an alchemical term for liquids that dissolve solids, metaphorically linked to biological cycles</term> composed of acidic spirits containing a metallic tincture within them; in this present category, we use the "bodies" of these spirits so that we may better prepare the solvents by degree. For example, the Tincture extracted from the dried body of Vitriol <note>Vitriol refers to sulfate salts; here it likely refers to green vitriol or iron sulfate</note> by distilling it with the <term>philosophical spirit of wine: a highly rectified and purified alcohol used as a base for many alchemical processes</term> is an Essence. This Essence, being dissolved in its own acid during that same distillation, produces a solvent of this kind; whereas in the preceding [category], that tiny amount of copper—dissolved or contained within common spirit of Vitriol and driven out by the violence of the fire—is reduced by the philosophical spirit of wine not into an Essence but into a <term>magistery: a preparation where the medicinal or chemical virtues are extracted while retaining the substance's bulk, unlike an essence which is more refined</term>, which is less effective due to the smallness of its mass as well as its Tincture.*

*The present Oil of Vitriol <note>Concentrated sulfuric acid</note> holds a high place among the Secrets of Basil <note>original: "Arcana Basilii," referring to Basil Valentine, a legendary 15th-century alchemist</note>, for which reason we shall weigh its very clear description a little more precisely, so that we may illuminate the more obscure passages with its fuller light. He instructs that **Roman Vitriol** <term>Roman Vitriol: Historically, this usually refers to high-quality copper sulfate (blue vitriol) or iron sulfate (green vitriol) used as a starting material in alchemical operations.</term> be purified through various dissolutions and coagulations. For the "earthiness" that settles at the bottom during the dissolution of Vitriol is not actually waste, but rather copper that is less dissolved than the rest, having been left behind because the acid was too heavily diluted with common water. He reduced not only natural Vitriol into oils of this kind, but also artificial varieties manufactured from metals. Note that the **solvent** <term>menstruum: a solvent or liquid medium used for extractions.</term> must be rectified seven times by distillation, always discarding the dregs before it is put to use.

*Sometimes, besides the ingredients of **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis: "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid.</term> and cinnabar, he also added calcined **tartar** <term>tartar: potassium bitartrate deposits from wine barrels, "calcined" or burnt to a white ash to create a caustic alkali.</term>. Thus,*

**Burning water of life** <note>original: "aquam vitæ ardentem"</note> of such strength that it may set fire to a linen cloth <note>A common historical test for purity; if the cloth burned, the alcohol content was high enough to be "philosophical" or "burning."</note>. <meta>This page continues the instructions for Recipe 104, "The Stinking Solvent," which involves a complex mixture of alum, tartar, and cinnabar. It details the specific distillation process, timing methods, and the transition to high-heat "reverberation" firing.</meta>

( 475 )

...of rock alum <note>original: "rochæ"; likely referring to *alumen rochae*, a high-quality alum</note> cleared of moisture and dried; one pound of all the aforementioned ingredients; and half a pound each of white calcined **tartar** <term>tartar: potassium bitartrate deposits from wine barrels, "calcined" or burnt to a white ash to create a caustic alkali.</term> and cinnabar. Grind each one individually and pass them through a sieve. Afterward, mix them and place them in a retort <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</term> and pour over them the aforementioned **Water of life** <term>aqua vitæ: "water of life," a term for high-proof distilled alcohol.</term>. Attach the receiver with the joints very well sealed, the luting <term>lutum: a sealing paste or clay used to make laboratory apparatus airtight.</term> having first been thoroughly dried.

The receiver should be large, like those commonly used for distilling **strong waters** <term>aquæ fortes: "strong waters," the historical name for nitric acid or other corrosive mineral acids.</term>. Once the luting is dry, you shall apply a light fire at first until the retort grows warm. Then continue the distillation at this rate: so that between one falling drop of water and the next, ten pronunciations of names or ten beats <note>Before the widespread use of watches, chemists used the time it took to recite specific prayers or names to measure intervals.</note> are interposed.

When it no longer distills at that level of fire, you shall increase the heat so that the distillation returns to the same rate—ten counts, just as at the beginning. You shall continue at this level until the distillation increases again, and finally, you shall increase the fire with wood, covering the retort on all sides with bricks above, so that it receives the fire of **reverberation** <term>reverberatio: a technique where heat is reflected or "reverberated" off the roof of a furnace back onto the vessel.</term>.

Take note of this: the retort itself must first be protected on all sides with strong luting from the start, before this distillation begins.

### *Chapter XLV. 3. Mineral Works* <note>original: "Oper. miner."; referring to Isaac Hollandus’s *Opera Mineralia*.</note>

<margin>Take</margin>
Two parts each of mineral antimony <term>Antimonium minerale: stibnite, the naturally occurring sulfide of antimony.</term>, burnt brass <term>Æris usti: copper or brass that has been roasted or oxidized in a furnace.</term>, saffron of Mars <term>Crocus martis: a red powder of iron oxide.</term>, and **cinnabar**; then take an amount of vitriol equal to the weight of all the other ingredients combined. When these ten days are finished, attach an alembic <term>alembicus: the cap or head of a still used for distillation.</term> and distill with a gentle fire at first, but finally for twelve hours with a very strong fire, so that all the colored spirits <note>original: "spiritus tincti"; the volatile essences that carry the "tincture" or color of the minerals.</note> can rise along with the aqua vitae. Repeat this labor many times, always distilling the water again with fresh materials, until it has become as red as blood.

*To these two recipes, we shall also add a third solvent of this species.*

->*Annotations.*<-

In the eighth category, common mercury <term>common mercury: Ordinary liquid quicksilver, as opposed to the specialized "mercury of the philosophers."</term> and metals were elevated into composite vegetable solvents <term>solvent: A substance, usually liquid, used to dissolve another; alchemists called these "menstrua."</term> either by the philosophical spirit of wine <term>philosophical spirit of wine: A highly rectified and potent alcohol used as a primary solvent in alchemical preparations.</term> or by some simple vegetable solvent. In the preceding twentieth category, dry coloring agents dissolved in acids are more easily distilled together with the philosophical spirit of wine into composite mineral solvents.

This present category, however, volatilizes <term>volatilize: To turn a solid or liquid substance into a vapor or gas through heat.</term> the aforementioned bodies not by the philosophical spirit of wine, but by mineral solvents, so that the solvents may be produced from them more quickly, with less labor, and of a higher grade. In the category immediately preceding, we distilled natural vitriol <note>original: "vitriolum naturale"</note>—which was either macerated in philosophical spirit of wine or, what is much more useful, dissolved in that same spirit and reduced to a refined vitriol <note>original: "vitriolum graduatum"</note>—into a mineral solvent. For the natural acidity of Roman vitriol <term>Roman vitriol: A high-quality grade of blue vitriol (copper sulfate), historically valued for its purity.</term> in its composition was not only capable of corroding copper, but was even strong enough to dissolve the philosophical spirit of wine in the preparation of the said solvent; here, however, the matter is different in artificial vitriols; for the dry bodies of metals in their dissolutions—

Dissolve it into pure water; if it leaves any **dregs** <note>original: "fæces"; the insoluble impurities</note>, gently pour off the liquid from the top. **Congeal** <note>crystallize by evaporating the liquid or cooling it</note> it again and again, until it leaves no more dregs. Now take your **sublimated mercury** <note>the white, fibrous material produced on the previous page</note>, your **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note>, and your clear salt. Grind them together while dry upon a **marble slab** <note>a flat stone used for fine grinding of chemical ingredients</note>. Put all the ground material into a glass bowl, place it on a tripod or in a **calcining furnace** <note>a furnace designed for high-heat roasting of materials</note>, and let it stand there for six weeks. Apply heat throughout that time, just as if you were keeping **lead melted** <note>a specific temperature reference, roughly 327°C, maintaining a constant liquid state without boiling</note> without it solidifying.

When those six weeks have passed, let it cool. Then place it in a **cold cellar** <note>a damp, cool underground room used to encourage deliquescence</note> and cover it with a linen cloth so that no dust falls in. Within a space of six or eight days, it will be completely dissolved into a clear water. You should know that this is the **Philosophers’ clear vinegar** <note>original: "Philosophorum clarum acetum"</note>; for when the authors write of "our vinegar," they mean this water, and when they speak of **Philosophers’ Mercury** <note>original: "mercurium Philosophorum"</note>, they mean this water. It is their vinegar about which they write and speak so miraculously.

1. *Metals and minerals volatilized by simple mineral **solvents** <term>menstrua; powerful liquids used to dissolve solid matter</term> are solvents of this kind.*

4. *These solvents, being mineral or acidic, are superior in alchemical works to the vegetable solvents of the eighth genus themselves, because they are stronger.*

8. These solvents, like the others, become sweet by **digesting** <term>digestion; a process of applying gentle, consistent heat over a long period</term> and are transmuted into solvents of the eighth genus.

My son, I will now teach you how to prepare the stone which God gives to us freely. Know that this is prepared in various ways, but I will teach you the method I learned from my Father.

Take a sufficient quantity of the stone which God gives us freely (*Vitriol of Venus* <note>original: "Vitrioli Veneris"; a copper-based sulfate</note>), dissolve it in distilled vinegar (*philosophical vinegar* <note>original: "philosophico"; a high-potency alchemical solvent</note>) without letting the dregs settle; carefully pour off the dissolved liquid from the dregs and filter it; draw off the vinegar with a gentle heat so that the material remains dry. # On the Work of the Second Book of the Revelation #

<margin>Take.</margin> **Common copper**, from which you should make **verdigris** <term>Verdigris; the green pigment or crust (copper acetate) that forms on copper when it is exposed to acetic acid or vinegar.</term> in the usual way; grind this, and pour over it a good quantity of **distilled vinegar** (*philosophical, or vinegar mixed with philosophical spirit of wine*) <note>original: "philosophici, sive aceti cum spiritu vini phil. mixti." In alchemy, "philosophical" reagents were considered more potent or pure than common ones, often prepared through multiple distillations.</note>. Shake it well, and the verdigris will be dissolved. Allow the dregs to settle; the solution will be very beautiful, transparent, and green. Draw off the vinegar in a **cucurbit** <term>Cucurbit; the lower, gourd-shaped vessel of a still that holds the liquid to be heated.</term> until it reaches a thick consistency, and in a cold place, the heavy **vitriol** <term>Vitriol; here, the crystalline salt formed from the copper and vinegar.</term> will crystallize at the highest grade. Dissolve this again in hot water, evaporate the water until it thickens, place it again in a cold place, and the vitriol will coagulate once more. This process of solution and coagulation is to be repeated a third time, and the purification of the vitriol will be complete. Let the **phlegm** <term>Phlegm; the watery, tasteless, and inactive liquid produced during distillation.</term> evaporate from this vitriol in a dish, and **calcine** <term>Calcine; to heat a substance to a high temperature to drive off volatile matter or to oxidize it into a powder.</term> it until it begins to turn red; then it will be sufficient.

<margin>Take.</margin> Then take pure **flints**, calcine them, and extinguish them while they are glowing hot in distilled vinegar; repeat this several times until they are well calcined. Then calcine them once more, and when they have cooled slightly, pour on heated vinegar (*philosophical*), and allow them to dry gradually. Of these prepared stones, take one part, and of the already calcined vitriol, take two parts; grind and mix them, and place them in a **retort** <term>Retort; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances under high heat.</term>

**Red oil of Venus** <term>Oleum Veneris; "Venus" is the alchemical name for copper. This refers to a highly concentrated, acidic liquid derived from copper vitriol.</term>, as heavy as lead or gold; as thick as blood, and of a fiery quality—that is, of the highest acidity.

Once this **oil of Venus** is prepared and diluted with common water, **iron** is reduced into a graduated vitriol. ### I.

## The descriptions of these solvents are to be understood
## according to the literal sense of the words.

*You will easily grant us your agreement that the Recipes <term>Recepta: specific alchemical formulas or prescriptions</term> of this book contain nothing hidden except for the philosophical Spirit of Wine <note>original: "spiritum Vini philosophici"; in alchemy, this is not merely common alcohol, but a highly rectified, "ennobled" spirit believed to hold the life-force of the substance</note> (whose use alone we promised to discuss in these present writings). Nor, however, is that spirit itself so obscure that it should not properly be called an "unctuous spirit" <note>an "oily" or "fatty" quality; alchemists believed this texture allowed the solvent to "grip" and transform metallic bodies</note> arising from Lull’s <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a philosopher to whom many foundational alchemical texts were attributed</note> "white and red wine," or from the constituents of the "fetid solvent" <term>Menstrui fœtentis: literally "stinking solvent," a common term for a sharp, pungent acid or distilled vinegar used as a starting base</term>. The remaining things that seem more obscure are technical terms of the Art, for the most part explained within the descriptions of the Recipes themselves, as being products or compounds derived from this spirit. Furthermore, the obscurity caused by either a very short or a very long description of a Recipe is merely incidental, and can be easily overcome and removed by any diligent student of the Art.*

## None of the aforementioned solvents can be prepared
## without the philosophical spirit of wine.

*Among all these Solvents <term>Menstrua: chemical solvents, named for the "menstrual" or monthly cycles of heating and cooling used to prepare them</term> of the Adepts given to you, there is not even one that does not have the philosophical spirit of wine as its base. There are indeed Solvents in whose Recipes the name of this spirit does not appear, yet the spirit itself* <note>The text continues on the next page, as indicated by the catchword "adest" (is present).</note>

### 3.
## Solvents can be prepared from any matter whatsoever.

*We have demonstrated that the aforementioned Solvents <term>Menstrua: liquid substances used to dissolve solids or extract their inner essence</term> are composed of various oily, dry, and acidic substances from the three Kingdoms of nature. ### 6.

## There are many Solvents.

You have observed various kinds of **Solvents** <term>Menstrua: alchemical solvents used to "open" or break down materials; the term relates to the cyclical nature of life and renewal</term> intended for various and distinct uses. Simple **vegetable** Solvents extract bodies rather than dissolve them; compound ones dissolve the whole and do not merely extract. What vegetable Solvents do, **mineral** ones cannot accomplish, and vice versa. From vegetable Solvents alone are **Medicines** <term>Medicamina: refined alchemical preparations intended for healing</term> fashioned, not **Poisons**; but from mineral solvents come only poisons, and **Antidotes** are produced only through the singular skill of the **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to the Practice of Alchemy</note>. Their diverse and mutually contrary uses allow for no single **universal Solvent**. The **philosophical Spirit of Wine** <note>original: "Spiritus Vini phil."</note> is indeed the universal matter of all these things, but among all the Solvents, none is given that is sufficient for every necessity. For this reason—unless you wish to call each one "universal" by the same name because they are all made from the **Spirit of Light** <term>Spiritus Luminis: a theoretical universal essence or "world soul" often identified as the underlying basis of all matter</term>, the universal basis of all things—the existence of a single universal Solvent must be denied.

<summary>This page concludes the description of alchemical operations and argues against the existence of a single universal solvent, distinguishing between the medicinal properties of vegetable solvents and the dangerous nature of mineral ones.</summary>

## That Certain Solvents are Corrosive.

*It is clearly evident from the previously mentioned **Recipes** <note>original: "Receptis"</note> that mineral **Solvents** <term>Menstrua: Alchemical liquids used to dissolve solids; the term literally refers to "monthly" cycles, reflecting the timing of natural processes</term> are **corrosive**, and therefore they dissolve bodies with **effervescence** <note>fizzing or bubbling caused by chemical reaction</note>. Do not—perhaps because you are not sufficiently instructed regarding the statements made everywhere by the **Adepts** <note>Adepti: those who have mastered the "Great Work" of alchemy</note> against **strong waters** <term>aquas fortes: nitric acid or other powerful mineral acids</term> and all corrosives—either despise these solvents or think ill of them. These are those very Solvents by which the ancient Adepts shortened the time and labor in the preparations of their **Tinctures** <term>Tincturarum: the potent, soul-like essence of a substance, often used to transform metals or create medicines</term>; and **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a revolutionary Swiss physician who championed the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine</note> claimed the Sovereignty over the **Secrets** <note>original: "Arcanorum Monarchatum"</note> for himself by a just title. He did this not only by applying the finishing touch to alchemical shortcuts, but furthermore by introducing these mineral solvents into medical use with such dexterity that it seems no hope of correcting any further imperfection of the **Art** <note>The "Art" of Alchemy</note> remains for his disciples, as will be demonstrated in the following books. Furthermore, these Solvents do not differ from **Vegetable Solvents**, except that an **Acid** has been added to them or to the **philosophical Spirit of Wine** <term>spiritui Vini phil.: a highly purified alcohol considered by alchemists to be a "living" solvent</term>; by corroding the **Dry** <note>original: "Aridum"; referring to the solid, earthy matter</note> and dividing it into smaller particles, the acid paves the way for the **Oily** <note>original: "Oleoso"; referring to the essential oils or "soul" of the substance</note> part, so that they might be able to unite and be mixed more quickly and better, which nevertheless*

### 8.

->*That Solvents are permanent; indeed, they are fixed*<-
->*together with the dissolved substances.*<-

It is clear from the previous descriptions of **Solvents** <term>Menstrua: Alchemical liquids used to dissolve solids; the term implies a "monthly" or cyclic natural process</term> that both the **Philosophical Spirit of Wine** <term>spiritum Vini philos.: A highly purified alchemical ethanol, considered the "soul" of the wine</term> and the **Solvents** prepared from it cling to the things dissolved in them. Indeed, there is no argument better confirming the excellence of **Solvents** than the fact that they are homogeneous <note>of the same nature or substance</note> and permanent with the dissolved substances; and thus, the dissolvers and the dissolved are transmutable into a **third thing** <note>original: "tertium quid"</note> which differs from both. So far, then, are these **Solvents** from being immutable that, according to the decree of the entire **Assembly of Philosophers** <term>Turba Philosophorum: Referring to one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts; here used to mean the collective wisdom of the masters</term>: *Namely, the **Dissolution** of the body is the **Coagulation** of the spirit, and vice versa.* <note>The alchemical principle that making a solid (body) liquid is the same process as making a vapor (spirit) solid; they trade states of matter</note> Nothing in **Adept Chemistry** <term>Chymia Adepta: High alchemy practiced by masters or "Adepts"</term> happens more infallibly. Moreover, you have observed this permanency of **Solvents** not only in the **volatilizations** <note>turning a substance into vapor or gas</note> of the Solvents but also in the **fixations** <term>fixationibus: The process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term> of some of them. In this way, you have the fixation of the **Philosophical Spirit of Wine** in the **Greater Circulates** <term>Circulatis majoribus: Potent alchemical liquids produced through "circulation"—a process of continuous evaporation and condensation in a sealed vessel</term> of the ninth and twenty-second Categories; but you will find more instances in the **preparations** <note>original: "Confe-", likely "Confectionibus"</note> of both **Medicines** and **Tinctures**...

### 11.
### *These Solvents are simultaneously the secrets*
### *of the third book.*

It is clear—partly from their recipes and partly more clearly from the secrets of the third book—that the **simple solvents** <term>Menstrua: Solvents or liquid agents used in alchemy to break down substances</term> are the **Philosophers' Stones** <term>Philosophorum Lapides: The legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and providing an elixir of life</term> that are not yet fermented. The **compound solvents**, however, are those mixed with the **masculine seed** <note>In alchemical theory, the 'masculine seed' usually refers to the active, sulfurous principle that must be joined with the 'feminine' mercurial solvent</note>, and are thus stones that are volatile and partially fermented.

### 12.
### *These Solvents are simultaneously the secrets*
### *of the fourth book.*

The recipes themselves indicate that these solvents shine by night and are therefore **perpetual lights** <note>Alchemists often sought "perpetual lamps," believing certain processed substances could emit light forever without being consumed</note>; they also provide the materials for **pearls and precious stones**, etc., which will be confirmed in the fourth book.

### Chapter XIII. Of the Philorcius.
<note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490) was a famous English alchemist. "Philorcius" refers to a specific work or section attributed to him, often linked to his "Bosom Book."</note>

> Without these **Waters**, we make little progress in this **Art**, and whoever possesses these Waters shall in no way doubt the completion of the **Art** <note>original: "hac Arte," referring to the art of Alchemy or the Great Work</note>.

## XXII. Compound mineral solvents made from simple mineral solvents and previously fixed staining substances.
<note>"Fixed" (fixatis) refers to substances that have been treated to withstand high heat without evaporating. "Staining substances" (rebus tingentibus) are materials capable of imparting a "tincture" or transformative color to a base metal.</note>

124. *Solvent of Venus by Isaac.* 514
<note>original: "Veneris." In alchemical code, Venus refers to the metal Copper.</note>
125. *Solvent of Vitriol by Isaac.* 518
126. *Greater Circulatum of Isaac.* 531
<note>A "Circulatum" is a substance that has undergone "circulation"—a process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel to reach a high level of purity.</note>
127. *Oil of Vitriol shining by night by Trimosin.* 538
<note>original: "Trismosini." Refers to Salomon Trismosin, the legendary teacher of Paracelsus and author of "Splendor Solis."</note>

## XXIII. Compound mineral solvents made from compound mineral solvents and metallic bodies.

->Unpublished writings of the Adepts, bestowed upon me for the<-

<note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy. "Adepts" are those masters believed to have successfully discovered the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

*Lully’s Book on Vegetable Matter.* <note>original: "Liber de materia Vegetabili Lullii." "Vegetable" in alchemy refers to the organic kingdom, including plants and certain organic salts.</note>
*Lully’s [Book] on the Mastery, or on the investigation of the hidden secret: from the illustrious Mr. Robert Boyle.* <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691) was a pioneer of modern chemistry and a member of the Royal Society, but he remained a lifelong seeker of alchemical secrets.</note>
*The Secret Book, or an Epitome of the Treasure of Health, by Edward the unnamed English Gentleman; from Dr. Dickinson, Chief Physician to the British King.* <note>Dr. Edmund Dickinson was the physician to King Charles II and King James II. *A Letter of Michael Sendivogius, from Dr. Faber, Physician-in-Ordinary to the British King.* <note>Michael Sendivogius was a famous Polish alchemist. Albertus Otto Faber was a German physician who served the English court.</note>
